tEn: Designers Embrace Vibe Coding and DIY Tools
tZh: 设计师拥抱氛围编程与自主工具
sEn: A survey reveals designers are happier with AI-driven workflows, and many are building their own tools, leading to new roles like brand engineers.
sZh: 一项调查显示设计师对 AI 驱动的工作流程更满意，许多人正在构建自己的工具，催生了品牌工程师等新角色。

consensus.en: Designers who currently vibe code report higher workflow satisfaction, despite widespread dismissive noise.
consensus.zh: 目前使用 vibe coding 的设计师对工作流程满意度更高，尽管有人对此嗤之以鼻。

consensus.en: Building internal tools and brand engineer roles is rising; designers create custom tooling for cross-functional needs.
consensus.zh: 内部工具和品牌工程师角色正在兴起；设计师为跨职能需求打造定制工具。

consensus.en: The future of design involves a portable context layer — a 'briefcase' of intent — carried across tools and agents.
consensus.zh: 设计的未来涉及便携式上下文层——一个携带意图的'公文包'——可在不同工具与智能体之间移动。

consensus.en: AI changes design workflows by enabling wider exploration and precision, but human steering and preserved friction remain essential.
consensus.zh: AI 改变了设计工作流程，带来更广泛的探索和精度，但人的把控和保留的摩擦依然不可或缺。

consensus.en: Companies must deliberately make room for AI experimentation, through hackathons or dedicated teams, despite cost and time.
consensus.zh: 公司必须通过黑客马拉松或专门团队为 AI 实验留出空间，即使有成本和时间代价。

contrarian.en: Better AI workflows are not fully automated; keeping friction lets designers fact-check intent and re-steer.
contrarian.zh: 更好的 AI 工作流程并非全自动；保留摩擦让设计师能核查意图并重新引导。

contrarian.en: Managers do more vibe coding than junior and mid-level designers, suggesting juniors may be excluded from AI processes.
contrarian.zh: 管理者比初级和中级设计师更多使用 vibe coding，暗示初级设计师可能被排除在 AI 流程外。

contrarian.en: Internal tools are not AI slop; they can be beautifully designed and elevate the builder's influence inside the org.
contrarian.zh: 内部工具不是'AI 垃圾'；它们可以设计精美，并提升构建者在组织内的影响力。

contrarian.en: Comparing models through one-shot prompts is meaningless; evaluation should focus on how they drive through iterations.
contrarian.zh: 通过一次性提示比较模型毫无意义；评估应关注在迭代中它们如何'驾驶'。

contrarian.en: It is okay to wait on adopting agentic tools; future mainstream tools will make switching cheap and easier.
contrarian.zh: 等待再采用智能体式工具也没关系；未来的主流工具会让切换成本更低、更易上手。

contrarian.en: Designers should enable cross-functional partners to do design tasks, rather than fear being cannibalized or replaced.
contrarian.zh: 设计师应赋能跨职能伙伴完成设计任务，而非担心被蚕食或取代。

turns.en: AI fluency is going to eventually just become like an ambient thing. I don't think we're going to like highlight that language forever. But I think right now it is an important language because a lot of companies are like, "Yeah, we want this designer who can come in and think. We want someone who knows what to do with the question 'what if' in a way that doesn't feel like it's from 2012, 2015, you know, 2018." That question seems to be being answered by like, "What are you showing that you're sharing?" Like social media is the new discovery engine right now. Like that is the way to — for better or worse — that is the way to prove that you are someone who is experimenting.
turns.zh: AI 流畅度最终会变成一种如影随形的东西。我不认为我们会永远去强调这门语言。但现在它是一门重要的语言，因为很多公司会说：‘是的，我们想要的设计师要能进来思考；我们希望有人知道如何应对“what if”这个问题，而且不能让人觉得那是 2012、2015，甚至 2018 年的思路。’这个问题似乎正由‘你展示什么、分享什么’来回答。社交媒体现在就是新的发现引擎。不管好坏，那就是证明你是一个在尝试、在实验的人的方式。

turns.en: Welcome to Dive Club. My name is Reid and this is where designers never stop learning. This week's episode is with Tommy Geoco who just finished visiting some of today's leading design teams like Vercel, Perplexity, Ramp, and we're going to go deep into everything that he's seeing around AI workflows and where design is headed next. And to start, I wanted to dig into his recent state of prototyping survey to figure out what details stood out the most.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Dive Club。我是 Reid，在这个节目里，设计师永远都在学习。本周的嘉宾是 Tommy Geoco，他刚刚走访了当今一些领先的设计团队，比如 Vercel、Perplexity、Ramp，我们将深入聊一聊他在 AI 工作流方面看到的种种，以及设计的下一站。首先，我想从他最近的《原型设计现状调查》入手，看看哪些细节最突出。

turns.en: The number one thing that stood out to me was that designers who are currently vibe coding are more satisfied with their workflows. I hear a lot of 'no,' and we both hear a lot of noise, man. And I did not expect that. I was very curious to see because I was like, "I know this is happening a lot. How much, and are people happy with it?" Because I assumed — I mean, we hear the stories like Meta incentivizing token layers or leaderboards, yeah. You know, and this like just like being crammed down the throats of employees. People seem to dig it in this survey and I thought that was really unique. I also thought — and I wish I had parsed this a little differently — but it's the people who are currently doing the majority, like so if a majority of their workflow is spent on vibe coding activities, it's design engineers, that makes sense. Lead principals, okay. But then it's like non-designer roles which might be students and researchers, then it's managers, and then it's like your general junior mid-level IC. And that part was fascinating that managers are doing more than junior and mid-level ICs. Either things are trickling down and people are experimenting and then they're going to pass it, you know, they're going to pass learnings down, which is kind of what we've seen on location, but it also might mean that like some managers or teams haven't yet made room for the rest of the team. I'm looking at a bunch of junior and mid designers that are getting cut out of the process as my data says.
turns.zh: 最突出的一点是，目前正在 vibe coding 的设计师对自己的工作流更满意。我听到很多‘不’，而且我们都听到了很多噪音，老兄。这我没想到。我非常好奇，因为我想：‘我知道这发生得很普遍。但有多少人这么做？他们满意吗？’因为我本来以为——我们听到过类似 Meta 用 token 层或排行榜来激励员工的故事，对吧。你知道，就是这样被硬塞给员工。但在这个调查里，大家似乎还挺喜欢的，我觉得这真的很特别。我还觉得——我希望能把数据解析得再细致一点——但那些目前占了大多数时间的人，比如如果他们的工作流大部分时间都花在 vibe coding 上，那是设计工程师，这说得通。主管级、负责人级，也行。然后是那些非设计师角色，可能是学生和研究人员；再是管理者；再是一般的中初级个人贡献者（IC）。让我觉得有意思的是，管理者的占比高于中初级 IC。要么是事情在往下渗，大家在尝试然后把经验传下去——我们在工作中看到的就是这样；但另一种可能是，有些管理者或团队还没有为团队其他成员腾出空间。我看到一大批中初级设计师正在被排除在流程之外，我的数据也说明了这一点。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, and, and, and that to me it's like, you know, I want to, I'm trying to give a little benefit of the doubt, but ultimately it's like, yeah, we need to make more room at companies. I don't know if it's trending in that way, but I'm starting to see more and more of that at certain types of companies anyway.
turns.zh: 是。是，而且，而且，对我来说，你知道，我想尽量往好处想，但归根结底，是的，公司需要腾出更多空间。我不知道趋势是不是这样，但我确实开始在某些类型的公司里越来越多地看到这种情况。

turns.en: I think it's interesting to think about the types of vibe coding, too, because the experience of somebody who is building all of these crazy processes or systems or files to get a tool like Figma Make or even B0 to look and feel like their design system versus somebody who's just every day they open up the production codebase and just start exploring and shipping. That is a pretty big chasm, too. Where I get a lot of people coming to me that are frustrated because they're trying to bend these tools to their will, and then there's another class of designer who really is — I mean, what's a design engineer and what's a designer if all you do is ship designs in code that ultimately make it into the product itself? That's the line. Like we don't even have the right language to talk about these different types of roles now.
turns.zh: 我觉得 vibe coding 的类型也很有意思。因为有的人会构建各种复杂的流程、系统或文件，让 Figma Make 甚至 B0 这类工具看起来、用起来都像他们的设计系统；而另一些人就是每天打开生产代码库，直接开始探索和上线。这之间是有很大的鸿沟的。而且有很多人来找我，他们很沮丧，因为他们想把这些工具拧成自己想要的形状。还有另一类设计师——我的意思是，如果你做的事情只是用代码把设计发布出来，最终进入产品本身，那设计工程师和设计师的区别是什么？这就是那条界线。我们现在甚至没有合适的语言来谈论这些不同的角色。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: And then he showed me that, and I'm like, "Okay, that kind of qualifies it actually. That's really cool." I'm seeing way more people trying to hire brand engineers. I never even considered that as a role recently. That is a thing. Brand engineers are on the rise. I think every blank engineer is going to be on the rise.
turns.zh: 然后他给我看了那个东西，我说：‘好吧，这确实够得上这个头衔。真的很酷。’我看到越来越多的人在尝试招聘品牌工程师。我以前甚至没想过这会是一个角色。但现在它确实存在。品牌工程师正在崛起。我觉得所有‘某某工程师’都会崛起。

transcript.sec: The Rise of Builders and Creative Loss

turns.en: Sales engineer, marketing engineer. You know, I feel like everyone is compressing to, for better or worse, builders of some sort.
turns.zh: 销售工程师、营销工程师。你知道，不管好坏，我觉得所有人都在向某种构建者压缩。

turns.en: I talked to Will King, design engineer at Snowflake, yesterday. He's like, "I get it. I love systems thinking. I like that it's all going towards this. You know, we're building factories. We're industrializing this even further. But there is like a loss of the free-form creative workflow, the exploration part that some people are just going to have to reckon with. And it's like, 'Where does that go? Does it just get eliminated, or does it sprout up in a different area? Like does everyone have to be a builder?' And I just thought it was an interesting question. I love the building and design systems and just the systems thinking side a lot. But I recognize that that's something to reckon with.
turns.zh: 我昨天和 Snowflake 的设计工程师 Will King 聊过。他说：‘我懂。我热爱系统思维。我喜欢所有东西都在朝这个方向发展。你知道，我们在建工厂，我们在进一步工业化。但那种自由形态的创意工作流、那种探索的部分确实在流失，有些人必须去面对这个问题。问题就是：那部分会去哪里？它会被彻底消灭，还是在另一个地方重新长出来？是不是每个人都必须成为构建者？’我当时觉得这个问题很有意思。我自己很喜欢构建、设计系统和系统思维这一面。但我也承认，那部分是需要面对的。

turns.en: How much time do you spend on that stuff?
turns.zh: 你花多少时间在那类事情上？

turns.en: It's more that the nature of it has changed, right? And I actually think about this a lot. Part of me is almost slightly self-conscious about it, but I do the vast majority of my — you know — messy explorations with AI now.
turns.zh: 更准确地说，是它的性质变了，对吧？我其实经常思考这件事。我甚至有点对此不太好意思，但我的绝大多数——你知道的——杂乱的探索，现在都是用 AI 来做的。

transcript.secZh: 构建者崛起与创意流失

turns.en: I feel like I've made the jump to the, quote, creative director, where I'm just working with AI to show me a certain thing 50 different ways. Then I pull the pieces I like, combine them again, and finally get to somewhere where I'm like, "Yep, that's good." Then I take that from paper, run it through Claude Code, and now it exists on localhost. Then I sweat the details and actually do the precision designing in code. Which is crazy, man. That's a very, very different workflow than anything I've done at any point in my career. Sometimes I wonder: am I losing some of the critical thinking associated with doing things manually—hitting Command-D and making tweaks myself? And yet I'm able to go through a spectrum of explorations so much larger than I could do in a day, and I can do it in minutes. I always see things I didn't plan on seeing. But that's different, right? It's just a different thing that I'm bringing to the table. These are different muscles I'm growing, and maybe different muscles I'm atrophying too, you know? I don't know. I'm kind of TBD on what the impact of that is for me even as a professional yet.
turns.zh: 我感觉自己已经能够扮演所谓的“创意总监”角色了：我只是让 AI 给我看一个东西的 50 种不同做法，然后挑出我喜欢的部分，再重新组合，最终到了一个我会觉得“嗯，这样不错”的地方。然后我把这个从纸面上拿下来，用 Claude Code 跑一遍，它就出现在 localhost 上了。接着我再抠细节，在代码里做真正的精确设计。真是太疯狂了，老兄。这跟我职业生涯里任何阶段的工作流程都完全不同。有时候我会想：我是不是在失去那种手动操作、按 Command-D 一点点调整时的批判性思考？然而我又能探索一个比我一天能做的还要大得多的方案谱系，而且只用几分钟就能完成。我总会看到一些本没打算看到的东西。但这就是另一种不同，对吧？我只是换了一种贡献方式。我在锻炼不同的肌肉，可能也在让某些肌肉萎缩。谁知道呢。这种改变对我来说会产生什么影响，连我自己这个专业人士也还是个待定状态。

turns.en: Just a quick message, then we'll jump back in. People are getting answers from tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity a lot more than they're clicking on Google lately. turns.zh: 很快说一个事，然后我们回到节目里。最近人们从 ChatGPT 和 Perplexity 这类工具获取答案的频率，已经大大超过了点击 Google 的次数。所以，如果你的网站不能被 AI 读取，你就在你的分析后台里看不到某种可见性的流失。Framer 刚刚推出了一个免费的 AEO 工具，它会展示这些 AI 系统如何读取和理解你的网站。10 秒之内它就能扫描你的网站，给出一个 AEO 就绪度评分，并指出是什么在损害你的可见性。我在 Dive Club 网站上跑了一下，只得了 50 分（满分 100）。还好 Framer 会告诉我需要做的修复步骤。所以，请务必花一分钟用 Framer 的 AEO 扫描器检查你的网站。你只要访问 framer.com/aeo 就能开始。

turns.en: Okay, get this. Jitter's latest release lets you build your own creative tools inside Jitter to make custom animations and effects. Just describe anything you want, and Jitter will give you custom parameters you can use to tune every single detail—whether it's 3D control, dithering, or even an old VHS filter. Once you get the effect where you want it, you can save it, share it with your team, and easily reuse it across projects. It really is as simple as typing out your ideas, which is perfect for someone like me who doesn't have a rich background in animation. Sometimes I even have Claude help me with the prompts. This feature has blown the roof off my creativity, and I can't wait to see what you make. Go to dive.club/jitter to get started. Now, back to the episode.
turns.zh: 好，听我说这个。Jitter 的最新版本让你可以在 Jitter 内部构建自己的创意工具，制作自定义动画和特效。你只要描述任何你想要的东西，Jitter 就会给你一套自定义参数，你可以用这些参数调整每一个细节——无论是 3D 控制、抖动，还是老式 VHS 滤镜。一旦把效果调到满意，你就可以保存、跟团队分享，并在不同项目里轻松复用。它就是简单到只要把你的想法打出来，非常适合像我这种没有丰富动画背景的人。有时候我还会让 Claude 帮我写提示词。这个功能真的把我的创意天花板炸开了，我已经等不及想看大家会做出什么了。去 dive.club/jitter 就能开始。好，我们回到节目。

turns.en: I started something two weeks ago where I'm forcing myself to have one day of no AI.
turns.zh: 两个星期前我开始做一个事情：强迫自己每周有一天完全不用 AI。

turns.en: No way.
turns.zh: 不是吧。

turns.en: Where I know it's a thing, because I've been building these open-claw systems, and it's really nice to get the context inside of that—like my intent, with inputs everywhere. What am I thinking? What am I working on? What did I vote? What was worth my attention on Twitter in this conversation? So I'm trying to figure out all these ways to get really meaningful Tommy's worldview context into the system. But then I'm like, okay, it's really nice because my outputs are really rich from this thing, and then I start to become a crutch. So no AI allows me to really think through things again. And also, I leave the day with more context that was truly authored by me, and I can feed it back. So it kind of has two purposes. And I'm seeing how you definitely feel it—like you, when you don't have it, the productivity feels really different. I feel stunted at first, for sure. Yeah, I think the biggest difference for me is I don't do near as much thinking from a blank canvas. My thinking is enough to give AI a pretty good set of guardrails for it to explore in the directions I want it to go. But sometimes, if I'm going to design a new layout, component, or section of a website, I'll just run a prompt to get AI to do a bunch of things on the canvas, and I won't think critically about that design until I see something. I'll see 20 things and then be like, oh, that's interesting, or, oh, maybe we should do this instead. But that's when my critical thinking starts—at the point where I'm already looking at something, rather than at a blank canvas. Maybe I'm typing words, drawing arrows, doing rough little sketches. That doesn't currently have a role in my process. It's just different. You have this spectrum from probabilistic to deterministic design, and I really like working over here.
turns.zh: 因为我在构建这些 open-claw 系统，所以我知道这个感受是真实的：能把我的意图这类上下文放进去，感觉非常好——而且到处都是输入。我在想什么？我在做什么？我投了什么票？这段对话里有什么是值得我在 Twitter 上关注的？所以我一直在想各种办法，把真正有意义的 Tommy 世界观上下文弄进系统里。但后来我就会想：好吧，这确实很好，因为这个东西给我的输出非常丰富，于是我就开始把它当拐杖。所以不用 AI 的那天能让我真正重新把事情想清楚；而且那天结束之后，我会拥有更多真正由我自己写出来的上下文，再把它喂回去。所以它有两个目的。我也看到你确实能感觉到这一点——就像你，在没它的时候，生产力感觉真的很不一样。一开始我真的会觉得很受挫。嗯，我觉得对我来说最大的区别是：我不太再从一张空白画布开始思考了。我的思考已经足够给 AI 一套不错的护栏，让它往我想去的方向探索。但有时候，如果我要设计一个新布局、新组件或者网站的一部分，我会直接运行一条提示词，让 AI 在画布上做一堆事；在看见结果之前，我不会去批判性地思考那个设计。我会看到 20 个方案，然后才会想：“哦，那个有意思”或者“哦，也许我们应该用这个”。但我的批判性思考是从那个时刻——也就是我已经在看着某个东西的时候——才开始的，而不是从一张空白画布开始。也许我会打字、画箭头、画一些潦草的小草图。那些东西现在在我的流程里没有位置。它就只是不同了。这是一道从概率式设计到确定性设计的光谱，而我很喜欢在这一端工作。

turns.en: Here's a question I have for you, because I'm really interested. We see so much noise online, and what's been really nice is to just ask people: what's your actual workflow right now? And you shared something recently—you had made these buttons, but it was like the AI had made them, and they were in the perfect design system of InFlight. So what was the process for you? What inputs were collected, to the point where you were completely out of the process and it just spun those up?
turns.zh: 我有个问题想问你，因为我真的很感兴趣。我们在线看到太多噪音了，而一个很好的做法就是直接问别人：“你现在的实际工作流程到底是什么样的？”你最近分享过一件事——你做了一些按钮，但那些按钮感觉像是 AI 做的，而且还完全符合 InFlight 的设计系统。那么你当时的过程是怎样的？它收集了哪些输入，直到你完全不在流程里，它就自动把这些按钮生成了出来？

turns.en: It actually ties back to a single Claude session I had maybe a few months ago. Like most Claude sessions, I started off saying, I have no idea what to do here. I feel like I should be using Markdown files and passing context through my codebase more effectively. I feel like you should be reading rule sets and gathering context more effectively given a prompt. And I wasn't doing anything, and I was like, what do I do? So I actually went out and found a bunch of Dan Shipper articles, a bunch of everything, and tweets I had bookmarked, and I just fed a bunch of stuff in here. I was like, consume this, help me think about a plan. I have no idea what to do. And it created this chart of nested context—Claude Markdown files throughout the codebase at different levels—that would teach it how to achieve certain things. And one of those is a set of visual rules for how I like components to be built. To be honest, I've never even opened that file. I don't actually know what's in there. I just regularly contribute to it. Like if I get an output I don't like, I'm like, yo, never do that again. This is what I want instead. And then it just goes and does something and goes somewhere, and I never look at it.
turns.zh: 这其实要追溯到几个月前我开的一个 Claude 会话。和大多数 Claude 会话一样，我一开始说的是：我完全不知道要做什么。我觉得我应该用 Markdown 文件，更有效地把上下文传进代码库；我觉得你应该能根据提示词更有效地读取规则集、收集上下文。而我当时什么都没做，于是我就想：我该怎么办？然后我真的出去找了一堆 Dan Shipper 的文章、各种乱七八糟的东西，还有我收藏过的推文，全都喂给了它。我说：把这些消化掉，帮我思考一个方案，我完全不知道该怎么办。然后它生成了这样一张嵌套的上下文图——也就是贯穿代码库各层级的 Claude Markdown 文件——用来教它自己怎么完成某些事情。其中有一组视觉规则，描述了我喜欢组件以什么方式被构建。说实话，我从来没打开过那个文件，我其实不知道里面有什么。我只是定期地往里面贡献内容。比如，如果我得到一个不喜欢的输出，我就会说：“喂，不要再这样做了，我要的是这个。”然后它就自己去处理，把它改到某个地方，我再也不会去看它。

turns.en: But I've done that enough now where Claude will know, okay: if I'm going to build a subtle interactive element, Fred probably wants me to use this tertiary style with this hover overlay blend that adds a little transparency on top of the gradient. And I just get that out of the box now. I get all my little inner shadows out of the box now. I never get things with borders anymore. I only get things using inner shadows to simulate borders. And it just took one pretty dedicated session. Like, I worked with Claude for probably two hours on this set of files, just refining it and feeding context into the system. And then from there, it's just taking a beat to tell it that something sucked, explaining why, and then saying, 'never let this happen again.' And I've just done that like 100 times. I really think that sort of black box — because I do the exact same thing — like I have not looked at much of my code in a long time, and my open Claude setup is very much like I know it's matching the intent based on the outputs. I'm not going to read a markdown file. Who has time for that?
turns.zh: 但这事我已经做得够多了，现在 Claude 会明白：如果我要做一个微妙的交互元素，Fred 可能希望我用这种三级样式，配这个悬停叠加混合，在渐变上稍微加一点透明度。现在这些我开箱即得。所有那些小内阴影，我也开箱即得。我再也不会得到带边框的东西了。我只会得到用内阴影来模拟边框的东西。而这只需要一次相当专注的会话。比如，我用 Claude 在这组文件上大概工作了 2 小时，不断打磨，把上下文喂进系统。然后从那里开始，就只是花点时间告诉它某个东西很烂，解释为什么，然后说“再也不要这样了”。这种事我已经做了大概 100 次。我真的觉得那种黑盒——因为我自己也完全一样——我很久没怎么看自己的代码了，我的开放 Claude 设置就像是我通过输出就知道它在匹配意图。我不会去读 Markdown 文件。谁有时间呢？

turns.en: But I mean, it's like a really fast, satisfying loop. And so when I hear people say GPT 5.5 is worse than Opus 4.7, I'm like, what does that mean? What are you comparing? Are you just saying you one-shotted a thing, and that probabilistic output you got from one versus the other on that given day was better or worse? Because that's not a very good way to evaluate it. How does it drive? There's this sense that you have to drive them for a little while. When you drive it with intent, and you're just saying, 'that's wrong, fix it, that's wrong, fix it,' and you do that a few iterations, I think then you have a good feel for how it drives. So I've never understood this one-shot mentality of 'I compared three of the same prompts.' It's like you just shot a bunch of probabilistic stuff. I hate those tweets, man. I hate those tweets. That's not even design. I get how that would be really appealing for somebody who's not a designer, but the fact that so much of the discourse from professional designers exists around which models put things out of the box in a more pretty way, or which models have less purple gradients — what are we doing here? AI gives me a level of precision that I've never had in my career, and yet we always are quick to say, 'well, AI slaps.' What? This isn't AI slapping. I'm making micro decisions that I didn't have a grid for a year ago, and it's only because of the abilities that AI gives me. It's really hard to talk about right now. You have to really talk to somebody about how are you using it? How are you evaluating it? 'Oh, you've gone down a rabbit hole that's a dead end.' Okay, let's pull you out of the rabbit hole first and make sure we understand: here's how you drive. All right, now that we understand what driving means, let's talk about some of the other things that are tertiary to it, that can inform. Because there is starting to emerge, I think, a right way to talk about — I know designers hate talking about using tools, but that's the moment we're in. How do you use these things? How do you install them? And so for me, it's like, how do I talk about agents right now? It's this headless design concept, I think. I think everything that you just described — how you created that button, these documents, this intent — I don't think there's a future where we're going from tool to tool and reinventing that over and over. All the hours spent just screwing in our intent the correct way is going to become just a briefcase you carry from one tool to the other. You know, like Ramp's Glass. They realized they needed it for their company, so they just built it internally. They shipped it this way. You know, someone who doesn't have this baseline education on how any of these work — it's already on their computer, and it just literally onboards them. 'Cool, you're now connected to Workday. You're connected to whatever data sources you need in a secure environment. Now you have your briefcase of context. Use it wherever you need to.' I think it's going to be the same in so many contexts, like design. That's going to be true for design. I feel like actually InFlight would be a great use case for this, if you guys decide to go that way. I was like, you're in my iMessage conversation right now. I think households eventually will have this, right? Like, I was talking to you at one point about this idea I had. You know, you call a product 'Hearth' or something. It's just the family's context layer. It's like your Life360 — for anyone who doesn't know, it tracks your children on their phones, because as parents you want to make sure they are where they say they are. Or it tracks how fast they're driving, because if you have a kid who's driving, you definitely want to make sure they're staying on the speed limit. You might have that data. You might have the family calendar. You might have all these things. And so now a family member doesn't have to vibe-code their own agentic setup, but they have a tool, they have this context layer. When all these tools become consumer-friendly, they can just connect to it, and it has context. I think that's going to be in every vertical. I've got to imagine.
turns.zh: 但我的意思是，这是一个非常快的、令人满足的循环。所以当我听到人们说 GPT 5.5 不如 Opus 4.7 时，我想说，那是什么意思？你在比较什么？你只是说你一次性输入了一个东西，然后你在那一天从其中一个而不是另一个得到的那个概率性输出更好还是更差？因为那不是一种很好的评估方式。就像，它开起来怎么样？你知道，有种感觉是，你得开它们一阵子。当你带着意图去开，并且你只是不停地说“这里错了，修一下，那里错了，修一下”，然后迭代几次，我觉得你就能对它的驾驶感受有个好感觉。所以我从来不懂那种一次性的心态，比如“我比较了三个相同的提示词”。那就像你只是发射了一堆概率性的东西。我讨厌那些推文，兄弟。我讨厌那些推文。那甚至不算设计。我理解这对非设计师来说可能真的很有吸引力，但事实是，专业设计师的讨论中有太多都是关于哪个模型开箱就能产出更漂亮的东西，或者哪个模型的紫色渐变更少——我们到底在干嘛？AI 给了我职业生涯中从未有过的精度，然而我们总是很快说“好吧，AI 真行”。什么？这不是 AI 行。我在做一些一年前我还不知道怎么做微决策，而这只是因为 AI 给我的能力。现在真的很难谈这个。你必须真的跟人聊：你是怎么用的？你是怎么评估的？“哦，你走进了一个死胡同的兔子洞。”好，我们先把你拉出兔子洞，确保我们明白：这是你怎么开。好了，现在明白了“开”是什么意思，我们再聊一些次要的、能提供信息的东西。因为我觉得，一种正确的讨论方式正在出现——我知道设计师讨厌谈论使用工具，但这就是我们当下的处境。你怎么用这些东西？你怎么安装它们？所以对我来说，我现在怎么谈智能体？我觉得这是一种无头设计概念。我觉得你刚才描述的一切——你怎么创建那个按钮、这些文档、这个意图——我不认为未来会是这样，我们从一个工具到另一个工具，一遍遍重新发明。所有花在把我们的意图以正确方式拧进去的时间，会变成一个你随身携带的公文包，从一个工具带到另一个工具。你知道，就像 Ramp 的 Glass。他们意识到公司需要它，所以就在内部造了出来。他们就这样发布了。你知道，一个没有这些基础认知的人——它已经在他电脑上了，然后它就真的引导他上手。“好了，你现在连上 Workday 了。你在一个安全环境里连上了你需要的任何数据源。现在你有你的上下文公文包了。你想在哪用就在哪用。”我觉得在很多场景里都会是这样，比如设计。设计领域也会如此。我觉得其实 InFlight 会是一个很好的用例，如果你们决定往那个方向走的话。我当时就好像，你现在就在我的 iMessage 对话里。我还想到，家庭最终也会有这个，对吧？比如，我有一阵子跟你聊过我有个想法。你知道，你可以做一个叫 Hearth 之类的产品。它就是家庭的上下文层。就像你的 Life360——给不了解的人解释一下，它会在手机上追踪你的孩子，因为作为父母，你想确保他们说的是真的。或者它追踪他们开多快，因为如果你有个孩子在开车，你肯定想确保他们不超速。你可能有那些数据。你可能有家庭日历。你可能有所有这些。所以现在家庭成员不需要靠直觉去写自己的智能体式配置，而是有一个工具，有一个上下文层。当所有这些工具变得对消费者友好时，他们只要连上去，它就有上下文。我觉得这会出现在每一个垂直领域。我敢肯定。

turns.en: Yeah, I think about that a lot, because I have visual language context right now. And then there's context from the code architecture — there's some business logic in there. I also have some running brainstorm context from Claude. Like, Claude understands what InFlight is, but it's not always amazing to hook in and pull everything in, or maybe it's a little out of date, or it's talking about this idea that I thought was cool six months ago that I don't really think about much anymore. I'm really interested in the idea of — you tee up InFlight, but gosh, whenever I'm riffing with Claude, I should be able to give it all of the feedback I've received as context. It should know that my co-founder Kyle always hates on the lack of negative space in my designs. He always thinks it's too dense. You know? That should exist. Or it should, if I'm designing a certain surface area, everything's going to be going through Claude or, you know, Codex, your tool of choice — it shouldn't matter, right? I love your briefcase analogy, but that model should be able to seamlessly tap into all of the decisions that were made about that area of the product a year ago. Right. And there should be no copying and pasting from you.
turns.zh: 是的，我想了很多，因为我现在有视觉语言的上下文。然后还有来自代码架构的上下文——里面有一些业务逻辑。我也有一些来自 Claude 的持续的头脑风暴上下文。比如，Claude 知道 InFlight 是什么，但总是不太容易接进去把一切都拉出来，或者可能有点过时，或者它在谈论一个我六个月前觉得酷但现在不怎么再想的想法。我对这个想法真的很感兴趣——你把 InFlight 拿出来说，但天哪，每当我和 Claude 即兴讨论时，我应该能把我收到的所有反馈作为上下文给它。它应该知道我的联合创始人 Kyle 总是吐槽我的设计缺乏留白。他总是觉得太密了。你知道吗？这些应该存在。或者如果我在设计某个界面区域，所有东西都会经过 Claude 或者，你知道，Codex——你选择的工具——这不重要，对吧？我喜欢你的公文包比喻，但那个模型应该能够无缝接入一年前关于那个产品区域所做的所有决策。没错。而且不应该需要你复制粘贴。
